approved: Criminal Code Amendment (State Sponsors of Terrorism) Bill 2025
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would create a new framework to list foreign state entities that Australia considers sponsors of terrorism.
The Governor-General would add entities to the list on the recommendation of the Australian Federal Police Minister, with the Foreign Affairs Minister's agreement.
New offences would target dealings with listed entities and financing state terrorist acts, with defences for lawful contact.
Creates a new Part 5.3A in the Criminal Code for state sponsors of terrorism.
Allows the Governor-General to prescribe foreign state entities as state sponsors of terrorism by regulation.
Criminalises conducting a state terrorist act, supporting or preparing such an act, and dealings with a listed entity.
Extends existing counter-terrorism orders under Part 5.3 to the new framework.
Amends other Commonwealth Acts to apply law enforcement powers to the new provisions.
Foreign state entities that engage in terrorist acts targeting Australia, and persons who deal with or support them.

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Famend%2Fr7382_amend_9c3bfff3-1ec9-475e-85a4-e3c4c89b684e%22;rec=0) introduced by Fisher MP [Andrew Wallace](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/fisher/andrew_wallace) (LNP), which means it failed. ### Amendment text > *(1) Schedule 3, page 53 (after line 20), after item 60, insert:* > >> *60A Paragraph 29(1)(baa)* >> >>> *Omit "under Part 5.3", substitute "in relation to Parts 5.3 and 5.3A".* >> >> *60B Paragraph 29(1)(bab)* >> >>> *Omit "under Part 5.3", substitute "in relation to Parts 5.3 and 5.3A".*

Argued that the Criminal Code Amendment (State Sponsors of Terrorism) Bill 2025 would create a framework to list foreign state entities supporting terrorism, establish related offences and safeguards, and extend existing counterterrorism powers; the coalition supported the bill but criticised its scrutiny.
